statement: In people who came to emergency departments in Europe after taking GHB or GBL and no other drug, those reported to have also taken alcohol, compared with those not reported to have, were recorded more often with reduced consciousness and, among those admitted to hospital, more often admitted to critical care; no difference was detected in slow breathing, intubation or overall discharge. The comparison is unadjusted and alcohol use rests on report. In 609 patients at 18 centres (2013–2016; 83% from London and Oslo; 183 without and 426 with alcohol), a Glasgow Coma Score below 13 was recorded in 49 in 100 of those with data and without alcohol and 59 in 100 with it (P = 0.034; unadjusted odds ratio 1.49, 95% CI 1.03–2.16), while a slow heart rate was recorded less often with alcohol (24 in 100 without, 16 in 100 with). Among the 219 admitted to hospital, critical care was used for 22 in 100 without alcohol (15 of 67) and 55 in 100 with it (84 of 152) (P < 0.001), about 8 and 20 in 100 of all patients in each group (editors' calculation); median time in hospital was 2 h 18 min without alcohol and 3 h 11 min with it (P < 0.001). Slow breathing (below 12 breaths a minute) was recorded in 12 in 100 without alcohol and 8 in 100 with it (odds ratio 0.68, 0.35–1.32; 21% of breathing rates missing), intubation in 4 and 6 in 100 (P = 0.32; odds ratio about 1.5, interval about 0.7–3.7, editors' rough calculation), and the two deaths (2 in 609) were both in the alcohol group, so the study could neither show nor rule out a difference in breathing or in death. In a randomized crossover study of 16 healthy adults who drank lightly and had little GHB experience, monitored in a hospital research unit, blood oxygen saturation fell most with both together, by a mean of 2.12 percentage points from baseline at 90 minutes, more than with placebo, with GHB alone (P = 0.027) or with ethanol alone (P = 0.013). The patient data come from emergency departments only, with no amounts, timing or product (GHB, GBL and 1,4-butanediol pooled), alcohol by report, toxicology in 6% of patients, no adjustment for age, sex or centre, about 33 uncorrected comparisons and missing values for several measures; the volunteer study is small, used one fixed combination, and measured oxygen saturation, a different outcome. Whether alcohol causes the differences, at what amounts, and the risk to breathing and life were not shown.
plain: Does alcohol with GHB make breathing or consciousness worse? In a European study of 609 emergency room patients who had taken GHB or GBL and no other drug, 59 in 100 of those who had also had alcohol were less awake (a Glasgow Coma Score under 13), against 49 in 100 of those who had not. Of those kept in hospital, 55 in 100 with alcohol went to critical care, against 22 in 100 without. No difference was found in slow breathing or in needing a breathing tube, but the study could not rule one out; two people died, both had alcohol. In a small study of 16 healthy volunteers, blood oxygen fell a little more with both drugs than with either alone. In the emergency room study, alcohol use was by report and the amounts taken were not known.
population: People presenting to emergency departments after acute toxicity from GHB or GBL and no other drug (609 patients; 18 European centres, October 2013–December 2016; 93% from six centres), and 16 healthy adults aged 22–34 who completed a US inpatient crossover study
exposure: Alcohol reported together with GHB or GBL (patients: report by the patient, companions or physician, or toxicology; volunteers: single doses of ethanol and GHB given by the study team under medical monitoring, study conditions)
comparator: GHB or GBL without reported alcohol (patients); GHB alone, ethanol alone or placebo (volunteers)
outcome: Reduced consciousness (Glasgow Coma Score below 13), treatment, critical care admission, hospital stay, slow breathing, intubation and death (patients); blood oxygen saturation (volunteers)
magnitude: Emergency department patients (Galicia, 2019; unadjusted; Group A GHB/GBL alone, n = 183; Group B with ethanol, n = 426; percentages are of patients with data): Glasgow Coma Score below 13, 49.1% against 58.9% (about 49 and 59 in 100), P = 0.034, odds ratio 1.490 (95% CI 1.029–2.158); bradycardia 23.5% against 15.7% (P = 0.027), odds ratio 0.604 (0.386–0.948). Any treatment 49.2% against 60.4% (P = 0.011); sedative drugs 12.8% against 20.1% (P = 0.034). Disposition did not differ overall (discharge 63.4% and 64.1%; hospitalised 36.6% and 35.7%; P = 0.842); among those hospitalised, critical care 15 of 67 (22.4%) against 84 of 152 (55.3%) and medical ward 76.1% against 43.4% (P < 0.001); of all patients in each group, about 8.2% and 19.7% (editors' calculation). Median time in hospital 2 h 18 min (interquartile range 1:01–4:11) against 3 h 11 min (1:56–7:13), P < 0.001; more than 6 hours 16.9% against 28.4% (P = 0.003). Breathing and airway: bradypnoea (below 12 breaths a minute) 11.6% against 8.2% (P = 0.246), odds ratio 0.684 (0.354–1.322), with 126 of 609 breathing rates (20.7%) missing; tachypnoea 14.0% against 14.7%; orotracheal intubation 3.9% against 5.9% (P = 0.321; 5.3% overall), odds ratio about 1.5 with an interval of about 0.7–3.7 (editors' rough calculation from printed counts and percentages); naloxone 19% against 21.5% and flumazenil 3.4% in both; no oxygen saturation is reported. Intubation rose as the Glasgow Coma Score fell (0.7% at 15, 2.1% at 8–14, 14.5% below 8). Two deaths (0.3%), both in Group B (P = 1.00): out-of-hospital cardiac arrest in two men aged 35 and 32. Healthy volunteers (Thai et al., 2006; randomized, double-blind four-arm crossover, 16 completers of 22; study conditions in a hospital research unit after an overnight fast: ethanol 0.3 g/kg, then 15 minutes later GHB 50 mg/kg as pharmaceutical sodium oxybate, which the authors call comparable to narcolepsy treatment doses, with a second ethanol 0.3 g/kg; average peak blood ethanol 71 mg/dL alone and 77 mg/dL with GHB): maximal mean change in oxygen saturation from baseline −2.12 ± 0.34 percentage points at 90 minutes with ethanol plus GHB, greater than placebo (P < 0.0001), GHB alone (P = 0.027) and ethanol alone (P = 0.013); GHB alone about −1.6 at 90 minutes, read by eye from a figure (approximate); saturation stayed below baseline for the 4 hours of monitoring; vomiting on 8 study days (6 with the combination) and 2 brief asymptomatic drops in systolic pressure to 71–73 mm Hg after the combination, none needing treatment.

Bradycardia 23.5% against 15.7%, P = 0.027, OR 0.604 (0.386–0.948). The other features tested did not differ. Group B were younger (31.5 against 33.1 years, P = 0.029) and arrived by ambulance more often (86.6% against 68.3%, P < 0.001). Table 2 and Fig 2 checked on the rendered pages.

evidence.locator: Methods › Euro-DEN plus Registry, 2nd paragraph; Study design, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Statistical analyses, 1st paragraph; Results, 1st paragraph; Discussion, 4th paragraph; Fig 1; Table 1
evidence.extracted: Secondary analysis of the Euro-DEN Plus Registry (22 emergency departments in 14 countries, 18 contributing patients; 17,371 presentations; 2,349 with GHB/GBL; 467 without ethanol data excluded; 1,273 with other drugs excluded; 183 and 426 analysed). GHB/GBL and ethanol status by report of the patient or companions, the attending physician or toxicology at the physician's discretion (done in 38 patients, 6.2%, finding GHB/GBL in 28.9%); no amounts, timing or product; each centre's principal investigator adjudicated cases with no central review; univariable tests only, about 33 comparisons without correction; six centres supply 93% of patients (editors' arithmetic from Table 1: two London centres 297, two Oslo centres 209). Not included: patients managed before reaching an emergency department. The author notes that low frequencies of some features may hide differences and that unreported co-ingested drugs cannot be excluded. Fig 1 and Table 1 checked on the rendered pages.

evidence.locator: Results › Pharmacodynamics › Oxygen Saturation, 1st paragraph; Abstract (Results); Figure 2 (image, read by eye)
evidence.extracted: Randomized, double-blind, four-arm crossover (placebo, ethanol, GHB, both; single fixed doses, study conditions) in healthy adults who drank lightly and had little GHB experience: 22 enrolled, 16 completed. Oxygen saturation fell with all three active conditions relative to placebo; the combination gave the largest drop, maximal mean change −2.12 ± 0.34 percentage points from baseline at 90 minutes, greater than placebo (P < 0.0001), GHB alone (P = 0.027) and ethanol alone (P = 0.013); saturation stayed below baseline for the 4 hours of monitoring with all three. Fig 2, read by eye (approximate): combination about −2.2 and GHB alone about −1.6 at 90 minutes. No interaction test, interval or baseline saturation is given.

evidence.locator: Results › Adverse Events, 1st paragraph; Results › Pharmacokinetics, 1st paragraph; Tables 1 and 2; Discussion, 3rd and 5th paragraphs
evidence.extracted: Vomiting on 8 study days (6 with the combination, 1 with GHB alone, 1 with ethanol alone) and 2 brief episodes of asymptomatic hypotension (systolic 71–73 mm Hg, under 15 minutes) after the combination; none needed treatment. Ethanol did not significantly change GHB pharmacokinetics (all P > 0.05; the study was powered to detect a 25% change in clearance). The authors describe a fall of about 2% in saturation as modest in absolute terms. Six of 22 enrolled did not complete.

risk_of_bias.note: The registry comparison is ROBINS-E high on its card (univariable comparisons only, with groups differing in age, ambulance arrival and centre mix; alcohol status by report, toxicology in 6.2%; selection of emergency department attenders at 18 centres, 93% from six; missing breathing, blood pressure and temperature data; about 33 uncorrected comparisons).

inconsistency.note: Not assessable: one patient study; the volunteer study agrees in direction on a different outcome.

indirectness.note: None as worded for the patient findings (emergency department attenders, clinical outcomes). The volunteer study is a separate indirect line (healthy volunteers, oxygen saturation, one fixed combination) and is not needed for the patient findings, so it is not counted in the arithmetic.

imprecision.note: Not scored: the claim words breathing, intubation and death as not detected, not as no difference; the interval for reduced consciousness (1.03–2.16) is wide but excludes 1, and its borderline significance is a multiplicity problem already counted under risk of bias.

publication_bias.note: Not assessable with one registry analysis.

large_effect.note: Not applied: odds ratio 1.5 for the main clinical feature; the critical care share is a proportion of patients admitted, which depends on who is admitted.

dose_response.note: Not applied: no amounts are recorded.

plausible_confounding.note: Not applied: amounts, centre and circumstances could push either way.

grade.reasoning: A registry comparison read in full, observational, so it starts low. Risk of bias −1 (see the domain note); other domains 0 and no upgrade. The same arithmetic applies if the volunteer study (randomized, would start high) is taken as the link for breathing: high, minus 1 for risk of bias (RoB 2 some concerns), minus 2 for indirectness (healthy volunteers, a surrogate outcome, one fixed combination) and minus 1 for imprecision (16 completers, no interval) is still very low. Relation: is associated with; the registry groups are unadjusted and differ, and alcohol and its amount rest on report. The claim does not say that alcohol with GHB raises the risk of stopped breathing or death: in the patient data slow breathing and intubation were not detectably different (with wide intervals and missing data), oxygen saturation was not recorded, and the two deaths are too few to compare. Status: single study. The patient findings rest on one registry analysis; the controlled volunteer study agrees in direction (a larger fall in oxygen saturation with the combination) but measured a different outcome and does not replicate them. No study read measured concentrations of both drugs in patients.

verification.flag_note: Not read: Rogeberg 2019 (culpability-design meta-analysis, 10.1016/j.aap.2018.11.011, open access); Dubois Appendix 1 and Rogeberg Appendix S1 (not in the PDFs); the older simulator and on-road studies of the combination (Robbe 1998, Ramaekers 2000, Lamers 2001, Lenné 2010, Ronen 2010), known only from how Hartman and Dubois describe them; Li et al. 2012, Elvik 2013 and Bédard 2007; the Hartman supplements and registry record (NCT01620177); the Thai companion papers on subjective and cognitive effects; Liechti 2006 and Miró 2017 on GHB with alcohol. No study read asks whether drivers or patients felt impaired (Ronen 2010 on perceived effects and Verster and Roth 2012 on drivers' own predictions are named in the Hartman reference list). The volunteer study (Thai 2006) is a separate, indirect line for the oxygen-saturation direction; no study read measured oxygen saturation or blood concentrations in patients.
